title: Psalm 53: The Fool Says There Is No God
summary: The fool says in his heart that there is no God, and the psalm describes a humanity gone corrupt: God looks down from heaven and finds no one who does good, not even one. The workers of iniquity devour God's people like bread, but God scatters the bones of those who besiege them. The psalm ends with a longing for salvation to come from Zion and for God to restore his people.
story: Psalm 53 is almost the same poem as Psalm 14, placed in a different collection. Its presence twice in the Psalter shows that Israel's songbook was assembled from earlier collections that sometimes overlapped. In Book II it follows the portrait of the deceitful boaster in Psalm 52 and widens the lens: the problem is not one liar but a human race that has turned away from God. It stands among David's psalms of trouble (52 to 59), setting personal enemies against the larger backdrop of human corruption and God's coming judgment.
historical:
The heading reads "For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath. A Maskil of David." Mahalath appears again in the heading of Psalm 88; it may be the name of a tune, or related to a word for sickness or sorrow, but its meaning is uncertain. Maskil probably means a skillful or instructive song. Psalm 14 is also attributed to David, with a shorter heading.

The differences between Psalms 14 and 53 are instructive. Psalm 14 uses the divine name the LORD (Yahweh) several times, while Psalm 53 uses God (Elohim) throughout. This reflects a feature of Psalms 42 to 83, which scholars call the Elohistic Psalter: in these psalms Elohim is used far more often than Yahweh, apparently because an editor or community preferred that name. The biggest difference is verse 5, which in Psalm 53 announces that God has scattered the bones of those who besieged his people, while Psalm 14:5-6 speaks of God being with the righteous and a refuge for the poor. Some scholars suggest Psalm 53 was adapted after a military deliverance, perhaps a siege of Jerusalem lifted, though the text names no event.
cultural:
In the Old Testament the fool (nabal) is not a person of low intelligence but a person who lives as if God doesn't matter, morally reckless and closed to correction. The story of Nabal in 1 Samuel 25, whose name means fool, shows the type: a rich man who insulted David and acted without regard for anyone. To say "There is no God" in the ancient world rarely meant a philosophical denial of divine existence, which was unusual then. It meant practical atheism: God is not watching, will not act, and can be ignored.

Scattering the bones of enemies (verse 5) was the ultimate disgrace in the ancient world, where proper burial mattered greatly. To leave bones unburied and scattered was to deny the dead honor and rest. The phrase about restoring God's captive people (verse 6) can refer to return from exile or more generally to a reversal of fortunes.
literary: The psalm moves from human speech to divine observation to a verdict and a hope. Verse 1 quotes the fool; verses 2 and 3 show God looking down from heaven as a judge surveying the earth, and his finding is total: "there is no one who does good, not even one." Verse 4 turns to a question of astonishment at the evildoers, verse 5 describes their sudden terror, and verse 6 closes with a prayer. Repetition marks the verdict: "no one who does good" appears in both verse 1 and verse 3. The looking down of God recalls the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:5) and the days before the flood (Genesis 6:5, 12).

outline.t: The fool's creed and its corruption
God looks down and finds no one who does good
A longing for salvation from Zion

doctrines.note: The psalm's verdict is universal: all have turned away, all have become corrupt. Sin is not only the act of a few villains but the condition of the human heart apart from God.
God sees what humans do even when they deny he is there. The fool's confidence is overturned in a moment of sudden dread, and God's justice falls on those who devour his people.
The psalm ends not with human reform but with a longing for salvation from Zion, from God's own dwelling. The answer to universal corruption has to come from God.

words.note: Nabal, fool. In Hebrew wisdom the word describes someone morally senseless: arrogant, godless, and destructive to others. Folly here is a spiritual and moral condition, not an intellectual one.
Shachat, to corrupt, ruin, or spoil. The same verb describes the earth before the flood, when all flesh had corrupted its way (Genesis 6:12). The psalm places humanity again under that verdict.

Darash, to seek or inquire. God looks to see "if any seek God." Seeking God in the Old Testament means turning to him in worship, obedience, and dependence. The failure is not ignorance but refusal to seek.

christ: Paul quotes the substance of verses 1 to 3 (from this psalm and its twin, Psalm 14) in Romans 3:10-12, as part of a chain of Scripture proving that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. His argument then turns: because no one is righteous, righteousness must come as a gift through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:21-26). The psalm's closing longing, "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion", finds its answer for Christians in the one whose name, Jesus, means the LORD saves, and Paul echoes this hope when he quotes Isaiah on the deliverer who will come from Zion (Romans 11:26).

hard.q: Is it really true that there is no one who does good, not even one? Aren't there many good people?
hard.a: The psalm is not denying that people do kind or admirable things. Its perspective is God's, looking down to see whether anyone seeks him. By that measure it finds a universal turning away. Some interpreters read the verse as focused on the specific evildoers described, the workers of iniquity, since verse 4 distinguishes them from "my people". Others, following Paul in Romans 3, read it as a statement about the whole human race. These readings need not conflict: the psalm describes a particular wickedness while recognizing it as the natural condition of the heart apart from God. The good that people do is real, but it does not make anyone righteous before God on their own.

questions: The fool in this psalm may believe in God in theory but live as though God is not there. Where do you see practical atheism in yourself?
Why do you think this psalm appears twice in the Psalter? What might it mean that God wanted this truth repeated?
The psalm ends with a longing for salvation. What does it look like to long for God to act rather than to trust ourselves to fix things?
